elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Inserted clause after 9.3: "Notwithstanding Section 2.1, Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience, in whole or in part, on thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Vendor" — covers both the Agreement and any Order Form, and partial termination.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: "on thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Vendor" — 30 days, written, no additional conditions, consents or fees attached.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: "and Vendor shall refund prepaid Fees pro rata for the period after the effective date of termination" — mandatory ("shall"), pro rata, tied to the post-termination period; consistent in direction with the existing 10.2 refund mechanic.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Second sentence of the inserted clause: "Vendor has no right to terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience during a committed term." No competing Vendor convenience right appears in 9.1–9.3 or 9.5 (all cause-based or non-cross-termination).

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The operative notice period is thirty (30) days, which is outside the 60–90 day fallback band but more favourable to Customer and satisfies the preferred element; the fallback is offered only in the margin comment, not in operative text.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the inserted clause imposes no early-termination fee or penalty and no such fee exists elsewhere (no "early termination fee" language in the cited termination sections), so no cap is required. Residual take-or-pay exposure under 2.1 is expressly left to the minimum-commitment rule.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Vendor is barred from convenience termination "during a committed term," so any Vendor exit without cause can only occur at term end (via non-renewal under 8.2); this is at least as protective as the fallback.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: Vendor is granted no convenience-termination right at all during a committed term, so no Vendor convenience notice period is engaged. (8.2's non-renewal notice period is not in the record, but non-renewal is not convenience termination.)

elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Same inserted clause grants the Customer convenience right; the fallback's only divergence is the notice band, addressed above.

reasons: Finding status is correct: Section 9 contains only cause-based exits (9.1 material breach, 9.2 insolvency, 9.3 Customer immediate cause rights) and 9.5 is a non-cross-termination rule, so with a three-year term under 8.1 and 2.1's take-or-pay "without reduction or termination rights," the absence of a Customer convenience right is walk-away territory and cannot sit at the fallback.

All four preferred elements are met in operative text — 30 days' written notice, Agreement or any Order Form, whole or in part, mandatory pro-rata refund of prepaid Fees, and an express bar on Vendor convenience termination during a committed term. The position is complete at the preferred level; the fallback level is intentionally not reached only on the notice band (30 vs 60–90 days), which is more favourable to us.

Minimal: a single concise insertion at 9.4 that adds nothing outside the preferred checklist. It deletes no favourable language, leaves 9.1–9.3 and 9.5 intact, adds no fee, consent or wind-down conditions, and does not attempt to rewrite the 2.1 volume commitment (correctly deferred to the minimum-commitment rule).

Preserves intent: cause-based remedies, the 8.1 term structure, the 9.5 cumulative-remedies and no-cross-termination rules, and the Order Form survival mechanic in 8.1 all continue to operate without contradiction; Vendor loses no right it actually held.

Drafting nit (not an element failure): the rendered clause carries no section number even though the comment calls it 9.4 — add the "9.4" label so the insertion slots cleanly between 9.3 and 9.5 and can be cross-referenced.

Drafting nit (not an element failure): the refund sentence says "prepaid Fees" while 10.2 refers to prepaid recurring Fees for the post-termination period. The new clause is broader and runs in our favour, but consider "and, without limiting Section 10.2, Vendor shall refund…" to foreclose a Vendor argument that 10.2 narrows the convenience refund.

Watch-item for the drafter: the unqualified "Notwithstanding Section 2.1" opener makes the exit operative but leaves it arguable whether accrued or future take-or-pay liability survives termination. If we want certainty, state expressly whether the annual USD 2,000,000 commitment ceases to accrue from the effective date of termination — but keep that in the minimum-commitment redline rather than duplicating it here.
